##### **1.2 Core AI Subfields and the Turing Test Framework** Russell and Norvig define artificial intelligence along six foundational subfields that together provide the operational capabilities required for an agent to act humanly. These disciplines partition the broader challenge of intelligence into distinct computational requirements: * **Natural Language Processing (NLP):** Enables an agent to comprehend, generate, and communicate in human languages. * **Knowledge Representation:** Provides formal structures to store internal beliefs, facts, and perceptual inputs before and during computation. * **Automated Reasoning:** Executes logical inference to interrogate stored assertions, answer queries, solve problems, and deduce valid conclusions. * **Machine Learning:** Allows an agent to adapt to novel circumstances, extract statistical regularities, and extrapolate patterns from data without explicit manual reprogramming. * **Computer Vision:** Processes visual inputs and sensory feeds to recognise patterns, estimate physical geometry, and identify external entities. * **Robotics:** Controls mechanical actuators to physically navigate spatial terrain and manipulate objects in the environment. The operational benchmark for acting humanly originates from Alan Turing’s imitation game, structured into two testing regimes based on sensory modality and physical grounding: The **Standard Turing Test** assesses conversational competence across a blind communication channel (historically a teletype interface). Because the interrogator evaluates the machine purely through textual dialogue without physical or visual cues, the test isolates cognitive and symbolic processing from physical embodiment. Passing the Standard Turing Test necessitates exactly four subfields: **Natural Language Processing** (to parse and generate text), **Knowledge Representation** (to store linguistic facts and concepts), **Automated Reasoning** (to construct coherent arguments and inferences), and **Machine Learning** (to adapt dynamically to the interrogator's conversational drift). The **Full Turing Test** removes the blind interface barrier by adding physical observation and object interaction. The interrogator directly presents physical artifacts, tests visual recognition across an optical feed, and tasks the candidate with manipulating objects or navigating an obstacle course. Consequently, passing the Full Turing Test requires all six subfields: the four cognitive disciplines of the standard test, augmented by **Computer Vision** (perceiving the physical environment and incoming visual cues) and **Robotics** (physically grasping, moving, and navigating in three-dimensional space). ```{mermaid} %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'Helvetica', 'primaryColor': '#e8f4f8', 'primaryTextColor': '#1f2d3d', 'primaryBorderColor': '#355c7d', 'lineColor': '#355c7d', 'secondaryColor': '#d6eef5', 'tertiaryColor': '#fff3cd', 'background': '#ffffff', 'mainBkg': '#e8f4f8', 'secondBkg': '#d6eef5', 'tertiaryBkg': '#fff3cd', 'clusterBkg': '#f9fbfd', 'clusterBorder': '#355c7d', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#ffffff' }}}%% %%| fig-cap: "Mapping the six core AI subfields to the Standard and Full Turing Test evaluation boundaries." %%| fig-width: 7 %%| fig-height: 4 flowchart TB subgraph STT["Standard Turing Test (Blind Text Modality)"] NLP["Natural Language Processing
Human text exchange"] KR["Knowledge Representation
Fact and concept storage"] AR["Automated Reasoning
Deduction and inference"] ML["Machine Learning
Adaptation and pattern detection"] end subgraph FTT["Full Turing Test Additions (Physical Grounding)"] CV["Computer Vision
Visual scene perception"] ROB["Robotics
Physical actuation and navigation"] end STT --> FTT ``` Under this taxonomy, the Standard Turing Test verifies symbolic, statistical, and reasoning capability inside disembodied systems, whereas the Full Turing Test verifies embodied agents capable of sensory perception and environmental interaction.
